title: Controllability and Observability
intro: Two questions decide what a state-space model lets you do. Controllability asks whether the input can push the state to wherever you like; observability asks whether the output carries enough to tell you what the state is. Each has a rank test that takes a minute by hand, each fails for a reason you can picture, and together they say when a transfer function tells the whole story and when it hides a mode.

blocks.text: Two questions

You have a system $x' = Ax + Bu$, $y = Cx$ and two things you may want to do with it. First, steer: pick a target state and find an input that takes the system there. Second, look: watch only $y$ for a while and say what the state was. Neither is guaranteed. Think of two tanks in a row, where tank 1 drains into tank 2. If water is poured into tank 1 you can set both levels, but if it is poured into tank 2 you can never change tank 1, because water does not flow upstream. And if the only gauge is on tank 1, its reading never tells you anything about tank 2. The first failure is a lack of controllability, the second of observability. They are separate defects, and the viewers have a preset for each.

The precise definitions are short. The system is controllable if, from $x(0) = 0$, some input brings the state to any chosen target $x_f$ in finite time. (For a linear time-invariant system the choice of time and of starting state makes no difference.) It is observable if the output $y(t)$ over some finite interval, together with the known input, fixes the starting state $x(0)$ uniquely. Once you know $x(0)$ and the input, you can compute the state at every later time, so observable means the state can be recovered.
A mode the input cannot reach

The simplest failure is a system that is really two systems side by side. Take the first hidden-mode preset: $A = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -2)$, $B = (1, 0)$, $C = (1, 1)$. Written out, the equations do not mix:

blocks.tex: x_1' = -x_1 + u, \qquad x_2' = -2x_2, \qquad y = x_1 + x_2

blocks.text: The input drives $x_1$ only. The second state obeys $x_2' = -2x_2$ whatever you do: it decays as $x_2(0)\,e^{-2t}$, and from rest it stays exactly zero. No input can set $x_2$ to a chosen value, so the system is not controllable.

blocks.text: The preset 'hidden mode: the input misses one' with a unit step from rest. In the time plot the blue $x_1$ rises towards 1 with a time constant of 1 s, and the amber $x_2$ is a flat line at zero the whole time. The thick red $y$ lies under the blue curve, because $y = x_1 + x_2 = x_1$. In the state plane the path runs along the horizontal axis from the origin to the red + 'rest' at $(1, 0)$: it never leaves it. The readout says 'Not controllable, observable. At t = 5 s: x = (0.99, 0.00), y = 0.993'. Now set x₂(0) to 1: the amber curve starts at 1 and decays on its own as $e^{-2t}$, the same with or without the step. The input has no hold on it.
The test: the controllability matrix

A rank test finds this without looking at the equations by eye. Over a short time the input pushes the state along the columns of $B$. As the state moves, $A$ turns each push into new directions: the state velocity $Ax$ has a piece $AB$ in it, then $A^2B$, and so on. So the directions the input can reach are the span of $B, AB, A^2B, \ldots$. The powers stop being useful after $A^{n-1}B$, because the Cayley–Hamilton theorem says that $A^n$ is a combination of $I, A, \ldots, A^{n-1}$ (it satisfies its own characteristic equation), and so every higher power adds nothing new. Collect the useful ones as columns:

This is the Kalman rank condition for controllability. For two states $\mathcal{C} = (B\ \ AB)$, a $2 \times 2$ matrix, which has full rank exactly when its determinant is not zero, that is, when $B$ and $AB$ do not lie on a common line. Worked for the viewers' systems:

items: Mass, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0, 1)$: $AB = (1, -1)$ (the second column of $A$). $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, determinant $0 \cdot (-1) - 1 \cdot 1 = -1$. Rank 2: controllable.

Pendulum, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (0, 1)$: $AB = (1, 0)$. $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, determinant $-1$. Controllable: even the unstable pendulum can be steered.

First hidden-mode preset, $A = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -2)$, $B = (1, 0)$: $AB = (-1, 0)$. $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, a zero row, determinant 0, rank 1. Not controllable, as the viewer's readout says.

Second hidden-mode preset, $B = (1, 1)$: $AB = (-1, -2)$. $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, determinant $-2 + 1 = -1$. Controllable. Both modes get some input, though with different weights.

blocks.text: Why does the rank condition fail exactly when something is out of reach? The cleanest picture is a combination of states that moves by itself. Suppose a row vector $w^{\top}$ satisfies $w^{\top}A = \lambda w^{\top}$ (a left eigenvector of $A$) and $w^{\top}B = 0$. Then $z = w^{\top}x$ obeys $z' = w^{\top}(Ax + Bu) = \lambda z$: it follows its own law and the input has no say. For the preset, $w = (0, 1)$ gives $z = x_2$ and $\lambda = -2$. The same $w$ gives $w^{\top}\mathcal{C} = (w^{\top}B,\ \lambda w^{\top}B, \ldots) = 0$: a combination of the rows of $\mathcal{C}$ is zero, so $\mathcal{C}$ does not have full rank. The two statements are the same statement. The converse, that full rank is enough to reach every state, is the harder half of the theorem; Chen proves it. What you need in practice is the rank test.
A mode the output cannot see

The mirror failure is a mode that lives in the state but never reaches $y$. The second hidden-mode preset is $A = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -2)$, $B = (1, 1)$, $C = (1, 0)$. Now both states are driven, but the output is $y = x_1$, and since the equations do not mix, $x_1' = -x_1 + u$ is a complete description of $y$ by itself. Whatever $x_2$ is doing, it never touches $x_1$. A look at $y$ alone can never tell the difference between a system with $x_2 = 0$ and one with $x_2 = 2$.

blocks.text: The preset 'hidden mode: the output misses one', no input, started from $x(0) = (0, 2)$. The amber $x_2$ starts at 2 and decays like $e^{-2t}$, and the path in the state plane runs straight down the vertical axis to the origin. The thick red $y$ is a flat line at zero: the whole motion is invisible at the output. The readout ends 'At t = 5 s: x = (0.00, 0.00), y = 0.000' and says 'Controllable, not observable'. Change Input to unit step and x₂(0) to 0: now the amber curve rises to 0.5 and the path ends at the red + 'rest' at $(1, 0.5)$, while $y$ follows the blue $x_1$ up to 1. The output reads $x_1$ and says nothing about the 0.5.

The test, again from the equations. With no input, $y = Cx$, and each derivative brings in another power of $A$: $y' = CAx$, $y'' = CA^2x$, and so on. Stack the first $n$ of them as a set of equations for the unknown $x$ at one instant:

blocks.tex: \begin{pmatrix} y \\ y' \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} C \\ CA \end{pmatrix} x \quad (n = 2), \qquad \mathcal{O} = \begin{pmatrix} C \\ CA \\ \vdots \\ CA^{n-1} \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{observable} \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{rank}\,\mathcal{O} = n

blocks.text: If $\mathcal{O}$ is invertible, the measured $y$ and its derivatives give $x$ at once; if not, a whole line of states gives the same $y$, and you cannot choose between them. (Derivatives are a poor way to measure in practice, since they amplify noise, but the page Observers: Estimating the State (#/math/state-space/observers) shows the practical way.) Worked:

items: Mass, $C = (1, 0)$: $CA$ is the first row of $A$, $(0, 1)$. $\mathcal{O} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Of course: $y = x_1$ is the position and $y' = x_2$ the velocity. Observable.

Second hidden-mode preset, $C = (1, 0)$, $A = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -2)$: $CA = (-1, 0)$. $\mathcal{O} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, second column zero, rank 1. Not observable. The null direction is $(0, 1)$, the $x_2$ axis, exactly the path in the viewer above.

First hidden-mode preset, $C = (1, 1)$: $CA = (-1, -2)$. $\mathcal{O} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, determinant $-2 + 1 = -1$. Observable: the output sums both states, and the two modes decay at different rates, so the sum can be unpicked.

blocks.text: Duality

The two tests are the same test written for transposed systems. Transpose $\mathcal{O}$: its columns are $C^{\top}, A^{\top}C^{\top}, \ldots, (A^{\top})^{n-1}C^{\top}$, which is exactly the controllability matrix of the pair $(A^{\top}, C^{\top})$. A matrix and its transpose have the same rank, so $(A, C)$ is observable if and only if $(A^{\top}, C^{\top})$ is controllable. This duality is more than a convenience: whatever you can design for controllability (such as the feedback gains on the next page) carries over to observers by transposing, which is how Observers: Estimating the State (#/math/state-space/observers) gets its gains.
What the transfer function hides

Both hidden-mode presets give the same transfer function. Compute the first one: $G(s) = C(sI - A)^{-1}B = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} \tfrac{1}{s+1} & 0 \\ 0 & \tfrac{1}{s+2} \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{s + 1}$. The second: $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{s+1}, \tfrac{1}{s+2}\right)\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} = \dfrac{1}{s+1}$ as well. A system with two states and a transfer function of first order: the pole at $-2$ is gone from $G$. The viewer prints the unreduced form, 'G(s) = (s + 2) / (s² + 3s + 2)', which equals $(s+2)/((s+1)(s+2))$, and its walk-through says that the pole 'cancels against a zero and G looks first order'. The zero at $-2$ and the pole at $-2$ are the same number, and that is what a hidden mode looks like in $G$: a pole-zero cancellation.

The general fact is that $G(s)$ is determined by the part of the system that is both controllable and observable. The other modes are real, they sit in the state and evolve, but $G$ cannot show them. That has one dangerous consequence. If a hidden mode is stable, as here (it is $e^{-2t}$), you may ignore it: the transfer function describes what you will see. If it is unstable you cannot. Take $A = \mathrm{diag}(-1, +1)$, $B = (1, 0)$, $C = (1, 1)$. The transfer function is again $1/(s+1)$, perfectly well behaved, but $x_2' = x_2$ grows like $e^{t}$ from any nonzero start, shows up in $y = x_1 + x_2$, and no input can touch it. The viewers have no such preset, but you can compute it in a line, and it explains why control engineers do not trust a pole-zero cancellation that happens to sit in the right half-plane.

A realisation of $G$ with the fewest possible states is called minimal. The statement is neat: a realisation is minimal if and only if it is controllable and observable, and then the number of states equals the degree of the denominator of $G$ after cancelling. Both hidden-mode presets have two states for a first-order $G$, so neither is minimal; the one-state system $x' = -x + u$, $y = x$ is.
What feedback cannot do

Controllability decides which poles state feedback can move. In the first preset, $u = -k_1x_1 - k_2x_2$ gives $A - BK = \begin{pmatrix} -1 - k_1 & -k_2 \\ 0 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$, an upper-triangular matrix, whose eigenvalues are its diagonal entries: $-1 - k_1$ moves wherever you like, but $-2$ stays. The next page State Feedback and Pole Placement (#/math/state-space/state-feedback) develops this.

blocks.text: The same preset with the gains set to $k_1 = 2.0$, $k_2 = 0.0$ (the values that step 8 of the walk-through chooses for it). In the s-plane panel (bottom right) the faint × marks are the old poles at $-1$ and $-2$; the bold × marks are at $-2$ and $-3$. The pole at $-1$ moved to $-3$ and the one at $-2$ did not move. The readout shows 'Feedback K = (2.0, 0.0): A − BK = [[−3, 0], [0, −2]]'. Drag Feedback gain k₁ and watch one × slide while the other stays; drag Feedback gain k₂ and neither × moves (only the dashed eigen-line of the $-2$ mode tilts): $k_2$ feeds $x_2$ into the equation for $x_1$, but nothing feeds back into $x_2' = -2x_2$.

If the hidden mode is stable, as here, you can live with it: the system is stabilisable (every uncontrollable mode is stable), and feedback can still make the whole thing stable. If the unobservable modes are all stable the system is detectable, which is what an observer needs. Stabilisable is the weaker, practical form of controllable, and detectable the same for observable.
The Lorenz preset in 3D

The 3D viewer has a system that fails both tests at once, in the same direction. The 'Lorenz system near the origin' has $A = \begin{pmatrix} -10 & 10 & 0 \\ 28 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -8/3 \end{pmatrix}$, $B = (1, 0, 0)$, $C = (1, 0, 0)$. The third row and column of $A$ are zero except for $-8/3$: $x_3' = -\tfrac{8}{3}x_3$ with no link to the other two (the full Lorenz equations have a product term $x_1x_2$ in $x_3'$, but near the origin it is a product of small numbers, and the linear model drops it). The input pushes $x_1$ only and the output reads $x_1$ only, so $x_3$ is neither reachable nor visible. The controllability matrix shows it: $B = (1, 0, 0)$, $AB = (-10, 28, 0)$, $A^2B = (380, -308, 0)$, all with a zero third entry, so the rank is 2 and not 3.

widget.title: Lorenz near the origin: a mode nobody can reach or see

params.label: System
options: a spin about an axis, and a decay

blocks.text: Lorenz near the origin, no input, started at $x(0) = (0, 0, 1)$. The path is a straight line down the $x_3$ axis, along the dashed line labelled $\lambda = -2.667$, and the violet $x_3$ curve decays like $e^{-2.667\,t}$ while the thick red $y$ is zero throughout (it lies under the blue and amber lines along zero). The readout says 'Not controllable, not observable' and ends 'At t = 0.29 s: x = (0.00, 0.00, 0.46), y = 0.000'. So $x_3$ cannot be seen. Now set Input to unit step and $x_3(0) = 0$: the path leaves along the plane $x_3 = 0$ (the violet curve stays at zero) and runs off because of the unstable pole at $+11.8$: the input cannot reach $x_3$. The walk-through, step 7, shows G(s) = (s² + 3.667s + 2.667) / (s³ + 13.667s² − 240.667s − 720) with zeros at $-1$ and $-2.667$, and notes that G has fewer poles than A after cancelling: the zero at $-2.667$ cancels the pole at $-2.667$, leaving $G(s) = (s + 1)/(s^2 + 11s - 270)$.

A last remark in one sentence. Every linear system splits, after a suitable change of state, into four blocks: a part both controllable and observable, a part controllable but not observable, one observable but not controllable, and one neither. This Kalman decomposition says that $G$ sees only the first block. The Lorenz $x_3$ is in the last.
Check yourself

blocks.title: Which way does the water flow?
blocks.text: Two tanks in a row: $A = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$ (tank 1 drains into tank 2). Test controllability for the inflow into tank 1, $B = (1, 0)$, and into tank 2, $B = (0, 1)$. Then test observability for a gauge on tank 2, $C = (0, 1)$, and on tank 1, $C = (1, 0)$.
solution: Inflow into tank 2: $AB = (0, -0.5)$, $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, a zero row, rank 1. Not controllable: the first state is out of reach, which says in algebra what 'water does not flow upstream' says in words.
Gauge on tank 2: $CA = (1, -0.5)$, $\mathcal{O} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & -0.5 \end{pmatrix}$, determinant $-1$. Observable: the level of tank 2 depends on the history of tank 1.
Gauge on tank 1: $CA = (-1, 0)$, $\mathcal{O} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, rank 1. Not observable: tank 1 does not feel tank 2.
blocks.answer: Controllable from tank 1 only; observable from tank 2 only.

blocks.title: Any push at all
blocks.text: For the mass, $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, let the input enter as $B = (b_1, b_2)$. For which $B$ is the system controllable?
solution: $AB = (b_2,\ -4b_1 - b_2)$. $\mathcal{C} = \begin{pmatrix} b_1 & b_2 \\ b_2 & -4b_1 - b_2 \end{pmatrix}$ and $\det\mathcal{C} = b_1(-4b_1 - b_2) - b_2^2 = -(4b_1^2 + b_1b_2 + b_2^2)$.

When is $4b_1^2 + b_1b_2 + b_2^2 = 0$? Treat it as a quadratic in $b_2$: $b_2^2 + b_1 b_2 + 4b_1^2 = 0$ has discriminant $b_1^2 - 16b_1^2 = -15b_1^2$, which is negative unless $b_1 = 0$, and then $b_2 = 0$ too. So the determinant is never zero except for $B = 0$.
So no matter where on the mass the force is applied (in this model, with any mixture of a push on the position equation and on the velocity equation), both modes are excited.

blocks.title: Find the hidden pole
blocks.text: $A = \mathrm{diag}(-1, -3)$, $B = (1, 0)$, $C = (1, 1)$. Is it controllable? Observable? What is $G(s)$ and which pole is missing?
solution: $G(s) = \dfrac{1}{s+1} \cdot 1 + \dfrac{1}{s+3} \cdot 0 = \dfrac{1}{s+1}$. The pole at $-3$, the mode $x_2$ that the input cannot reach, is missing. (Unreduced: $(s + 3)/((s+1)(s+3))$.)
blocks.answer: Not controllable, observable; $G = 1/(s + 1)$, the pole at $-3$ is hidden.

blocks.title: Duality in use
blocks.text: The pair $A = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -4 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$, $C = (1, 0)$ is observable. Write down the controllable pair it corresponds to and check the rank.
solution: By duality the pair is $(A^{\top}, C^{\top})$ with $A^{\top} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -4 \\ 1 & -1 \end{pmatrix}$ and $B' = C^{\top} = (1, 0)$.

$A^{\top}B' = (0, 1)$, so the controllability matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, the identity, rank 2. It is the transpose of the $\mathcal{O}$ found above, which was also the identity.

blocks.text: Sources and further reading

items: R. E. Kalman, "On the general theory of control systems", Proceedings of the First IFAC Congress (Moscow, 1960). One of the papers in which Kalman introduced controllability and observability.

Chi-Tsong Chen, Linear System Theory and Design, 4th edition (Oxford University Press, 2013). The chapters on controllability and observability prove the rank conditions, the duality and the Kalman decomposition.
Katsuhiko Ogata, Modern Control Engineering, 5th edition (Prentice Hall, 2010). Controllability and observability are treated in the chapters on state-space analysis and design.
Karl Johan Åström and Richard M. Murray, Feedback Systems: An Introduction for Scientists and Engineers, 2nd edition (Princeton University Press, 2021).
Gene F. Franklin, J. David Powell and Abbas Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems, 7th edition (Pearson, 2015).
